docs.title: SmartWilds
docs.text:
Integration, alignment, and release code for a multi-modal field sensing dataset

SmartWilds is a multi-modal sensing dataset recorded with camera traps, acoustic recorders, drones, and visitor photographs at The Wilds (Cumberland, Ohio) in summer 2025. This repository holds the metadata: Darwin Core tables for all four modalities on one Event hierarchy, with corrected timestamps and coordinates so they can be joined in space and time, the record of every defect found and repaired, and the code that did it. Raw images and labels will be released soon.

Figure 1. Sensor deployment across The Wilds: camera traps with viewing angles, Song Meter recorders, citizen-science photo locations, and drone flight tracks. Satellite imagery © Google.

Figure 2. The same three managed focal species (Sichuan takin, Milu deer, Przewalski's horse) observed by camera trap, drone, and citizen-science photography.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Imageomics/smartwilds
cd smartwilds
pip install -r requirements.txt
python examples/quickstart.py darwin_core/smartwilds-camera-traps darwin_core/smartwilds-bioacoustics

The quickstart loads the tables, applies a verification floor, joins Occurrences to their Events, and summarizes them by deployment and by class. See Using the data correctly before computing anything from the Occurrence tables.

docs.title: How LLM coding agents were used to document SmartWilds
docs.text: The SmartWilds documentation (the per-campaign data reports, the Darwin Core tables and their data dictionaries, the dataset cards, the supplement, and the defect inventory) was produced with LLM coding agents working directly in the project's file system, under the direction of the authors. This note records what the agents did, what they were given, and what we learned, so that the approach can be reused and so that readers know which parts of the documentation were machine-assisted.

docs.title: What the agents did
docs.text:
Inventorying the archive. The agents walked each campaign directory and wrote the data reports in field_campaigns/: file counts and sizes per modality and deployment, the metadata and log files present, naming conventions, and anything that looked wrong (a camera whose clock reported 2023, a deployment that ran out of battery, drone flights with no telemetry file). A human then checked each report against the field notes.

Summarizing the records. For every modality the agents tabulated the Darwin Core Events and Occurrences: counts per deployment, per taxon, per verification status, and per campaign; the date range of each table; and the share of records with coordinates, times, and media links. Those summaries became the inventories in docs/SUPPLEMENTAL.md (S2, S9, S12) and the counts in the dataset cards.

Finding errors and discrepancies. Most rows of docs/DEFECT_INVENTORY.md were first noticed by an agent cross-checking two things that should agree: the file inventory against the Event table (WAV files with no Event; a drone video never processed), the Occurrence dates against their parent Event's span (curated records that had bypassed the timestamp correction), the string nan where a date should be, duplicate identifiers after an annotation update, and media references pointing at a scratch workspace that no longer existed. The inventory records, for each defect, what made it visible; that column is in large part a record of these checks.

Automated QA/QC. The checks that proved useful were turned into scripts so they run on every rebuild rather than once: the read-only table audit (scripts/validation/audit_darwin_core_snapshot.py) and the release-build checks (dates inside Event spans and the study window, no sentinel strings, no archive paths, every media reference resolving to an included file, checksums for every shipped file). The agents wrote the first versions of these scripts and the audit reports they emit.

Drafting and maintaining documentation. Dataset cards, the data dictionaries (generated from the tables), the supplement, and this repository's READMEs were drafted by agents from the tables and the field notes, then edited by the authors. When a table changed, the agents were asked to find every number in the documentation that depended on it and either update it or flag it. The dated "before" copies and JSON audit records that accompany each repair exist so that this re-derivation can be checked.

docs.title: What the agents were given
docs.text:
Prompting with the documentation standards we wanted to follow, rather than describing the desired output from scratch, was the single biggest time saver. The agents were given, as context for every documentation task:

  • the FAIR² Drones Data Standard (template, quick-start checklist, and the KABR worked example), which fixes the section order of a dataset card, the Darwin Core Event and Occurrence fields to report, the platform and sensor metadata to capture, and the annotation and quality fields;
  • the Imageomics dataset card template, which the FAIR² template extends, and the Hugging Face dataset-card conventions it builds on;
  • the Darwin Core term definitions, so that column names, event types, and the verification-status vocabulary followed the standard rather than being invented;
  • the project's own field notes, sensor configuration tables, and processing logs.

With those in context, the agents produced cards and inventories in the expected structure on the first pass, and the review effort went into checking numbers and wording rather than restructuring. Giving the agent a standard also made omissions visible: an empty template section is a prompt to go and find the missing information (or to record, as in S8 of the supplement, that it is genuinely absent and why).

The guidelines are small enough to include verbatim in an agent's context or to package as a reusable skill:

Resource Use FAIR² Drones Data Standard, https://imageomics.github.io/fair_drones/ (TEMPLATE.md, QUICKSTART_GUIDE.md) Dataset card structure and required metadata for drone and multi-sensor wildlife datasets Imageomics dataset card template, https://imageomics.github.io/Imageomics-guide/wiki-guide/HF_DatasetCard_Template_Imageomics/ Base card template for biodiversity and computer-vision datasets Hugging Face dataset cards, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/datasets-cards YAML front matter and card conventions Darwin Core, https://dwc.tdwg.org/terms/ Term definitions for Events and Occurrences KABR behavior telemetry dataset, https://huggingface.co/datasets/imageomics/kabr-behavior-telemetry A completed FAIR² Drones card and processing scripts to imitate

docs.title: Limits and review
docs.text:
The agents did not decide what the data mean. Every repair in the defect inventory was chosen by the authors; the agents proposed candidates and implemented the chosen one with a before-copy and an audit record. Numbers in the documentation were recomputed from the tables, not copied from earlier prose, and the authors spot-checked them against independent counts. Where a figure could not be recomputed from the released tables, the supplement says so. Agent-drafted text was edited for accuracy and tone before release, and remaining uncertainties are marked in the documents rather than resolved by guesswork.

One class of text is never drafted: funder acknowledgements. Grant support language, award numbers, and the funders' disclaimer are copied exactly from guidelines/ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md; an agent that paraphrases or shortens them produces a wrong acknowledgement, and the review checks for it.

docs.title: SmartWilds camera traps: release note
docs.text:
The canonical camera-trap release is the smartwilds-camera-traps dataset (release build 2026-11-08). It contains 72,775 retained animal bounding boxes with original SAM3 proposal geometry, 19,785 camera Events, and the complete 235,778-image inventory. The canonical merged multimodal tables have 22,242 Events and 401,602 unique Occurrences.

SAM3 generated the original proposals. Resolve–Clear–Defer prototype triage used reviewed examples to classify or defer proposals, and label provenance is preserved per box. Every retained occurrence preserves original SAM3 proposal geometry; targeted taxonomic corrections to existing proposals are retained.

The full inventory remains available and its image-level occurrence counts are recomputed for this release. A zero count does not establish animal absence. Privacy fields retain screening evidence and record the human-review outcome. The 31 curated images flagged by screening were human-reviewed and approved for upload.

docs.title: Method citation
docs.text: The semi-automated labeling workflow follows Potlapally et al. (2026), Resolve, Clear, or Defer: Training-Free Active Prototype Triage for Ecological Detection Pipelines.

docs.title: S1. Extended glossary
docs.text: Term Source Meaning in this release What it is not Event Darwin Core A sampling act with a date, location, protocol, and parentEventID. Five levels in use: Project, SensorDeployment, AudioRecording, MediaEvent, ObservationSession. Not an arrival in a stream. One Event can contain 10⁵ arrivals. Occurrence Darwin Core One organism record at a place and time, linked by eventID. Usually one detection crop. Not an individual animal. Adjacent drone frames yield many Occurrences of the same animal. eventType Darwin Core The level of the hierarchy a row occupies. Not the modality; modality is carried by parentEventID and modality_type. basisOfRecord Darwin Core MachineObservation for every detector-derived row; HumanObservation for citizen-science and text records and for the 12 human-added drone starling boxes. Not a quality statement. See identificationVerificationStatus. identificationVerificationStatus Darwin Core Vocabulary differs by table. Post-triage camera traps: human-reviewed, machine-resolved. Drones and bioacoustics: unverified, validated, plus human-supported; limited-resolution for the drone starling supplement. Citizen science and text: verified by expert. Counts in S9.3. Not a confidence score. machine-resolved and unverified are both machine labels; a validated or human-reviewed record was reviewed by a person. dataGeneralizations Darwin Core States whether a coordinate is an observed position, a sensor position, a projected estimate, or a platform-telemetry fallback. Not a precision estimate; see coordinateUncertaintyInMeters. informationWithheld Darwin Core Records where locality precision was reduced for sensitive taxa. — Sampling effort Humboldt ext. Acquisition quantity actually expended, per modality: camera observation-days, recorder-hours, flight-minutes, visitor sessions. Not comparable across modalities. Not a detection count. Arrival systems One item entering a processing stream. Two layers measured: acquisition (image capture, WAV file) and detection (an Occurrence). Not a Darwin Core Event. Deployment systems One physical installation of one device at one site over one interval. Not a device. One device yields several deployments across campaigns. Duty cycle systems Fraction of wall-clock time a device was scheduled to acquire. Not uptime. A device can be on-schedule and dead. Detection systems A model output: a SAM3 box, a BirdNET hit. Not an identification. Identification Darwin Core A taxonomic assignment with a stated verification status. Not implied by a detection. locationID Darwin Core Stable identifier for a fixed sensor position or a drone session origin. Null for locality-only records. Not a comparable spatial sampling unit across modalities. Coverage systems Distinct (date, hour) pairs containing ≥1 Occurrence, per modality. Not area surveyed. Not detection probability. Campaign this release One field deployment interval. Three: C1 Jun 30–Jul 3, C2 Aug 4–28, C3 Sep 8. Not a Darwin Core term.

Three platforms produced three telemetry schemas with different field names, units (feet vs. metres for altitude), and gimbal-angle conventions. Fields consumed by the projection script, with their per-platform sources:

  • platform GPS — latitude_y / longitude_y
  • AGL height — height_sonar(feet) when available, else altitude (m) / altitude_m
  • heading — gimbal_heading(degrees) or compass_heading(degrees)
  • pitch — gimbal_pitch(degrees), with a configurable fallback when near-level
  • FOV — approximate per-platform constant

docs.title: S6. Drone ground projection
docs.text:
The campaigns were flown for population estimation and behavior, not geolocation. Platform GPS localizes a detection to a known pasture, which is the operative spatial reference. Per-animal projection is an optional refinement provided for completeness; no result in any of the three papers depends on it. Monocular distance estimation from a moving platform to moving subjects is unreliable and is not established practice in aerial wildlife survey.

Status Detections Share ok (projected position available) 247,340 77.9% invalid_altitude 27,306 8.6% missing_drone_gps 24,467 7.7% horizon_ray (camera near level) 18,324 5.8% out_of_range 122 0.04%

Method: convert the bbox bottom-center pixel to a camera ray, rotate by heading/pitch, intersect with a flat ground plane, project the offset from platform GPS. Dominant error sources: gimbal-pitch convention, terrain relief, altitude source, video stabilisation, FOV assumption, and whether bbox bottom-center is the animal's ground-contact point.

Camera-trap coordinates use the pinhole method from https://github.com/Imageomics/camera-trap-geolocation: bbox height → range, bbox horizontal offset → bearing, projected from the camera GPS. Assumes flat ground and a uniform 0.9 m target height — the dominant error term at a site holding animals from geese to Père David's deer.

Known analysis hazard. An internal audit found a spatial figure that plotted projected animal positions and platform-telemetry positions together without distinguishing them: 15.66% of 292,106 plotted drone points were platform coordinates. The status field was present and correct; the script did not read it. The release carries that status on every drone Occurrence (drone_georef_status in occurrenceRemarks, georef_status in detections.csv); any analysis of drone coordinates must filter on it, and examples/quickstart.py shows the pattern. No automated check of downstream analyses ships with the release.

docs.title: S9. Models, parameters, and measured accuracy
docs.text:
Manual annotation does not scale to sensor-network volume: human-reviewed labels are under 1% of the release and consumed the review capacity available. Semi-automated analysis is therefore the realistic condition, and we use current state-of-the-art models so that reported quality reflects what a practitioner adopting today's best tooling would obtain.

Labels were produced in two generations, and the released tables carry both. The first generation labeled every SAM3 box with a BioCLIP Tree-of-Life taxon; it still describes the operational drone table and the merged cross-modal snapshot. The second generation (October–November 2026) replaced the camera-trap labels with embedding-based triage plus targeted human review (S9.1), and added a seven-video human-annotated drone reference set with a manual starling supplement (S9.2).

Stage Model Role Visual segmentation SAM 3 bounding boxes on camera-trap images and drone frames Visual classification, first generation BioCLIP Tree-of-Life (TreeOfLife-200M) top-1 taxon with full rank hierarchy, top-5 retained; operational drone labels Label triage, second generation Resolve–Clear–Defer prototype triage over proposal embeddings routes proposals to human review and resolves the rest by similarity to reviewed examples; operational camera-trap labels Acoustic detection BirdNET detections with frequency bounds and offset into the WAV Water/lake masking SAM 3 lake/water masks for habitat-association analysis

docs.title: S9.1 Camera-trap labels (post-triage)
docs.text:
Operational camera-trap Occurrences are SAM3 animal proposals labeled by Resolve–Clear–Defer triage. The triage selects proposals for human review and resolves the remainder by similarity to reviewed examples; labelProvenance records the outcome on every row, with the triage round where recovered.

labelProvenance identificationVerificationStatus Occurrences triage_reviewed human-reviewed 1,760 triage_resolved machine-resolved 70,808 triage_forced_1nn machine-resolved 201 Total 72,769

Forced nearest-neighbour labels did not meet the triage confidence rules and may be wrong; exclude them unless label noise is tolerable. Box geometry is never edited (geometryProvenance = SAM3), even when the label was human reviewed. The table keeps only reviewed or resolved animal proposals: cleared and background proposals, boxes with a shorter side below 32 px, boxes overlapping the per-resolution ROI mask, and frames on the privacy exclusion manifest are excluded, so an image without an Occurrence is not evidence that no animal was present. Twelve taxa occur: milu (Père David's) deer, Przewalski's horse, Canada goose, Sichuan takin, trumpeter swan, killdeer, European starling, barn swallow, and the broad labels bird, butterfly, dragonfly, and insect.

A separate human-reviewed reference set of 2,067 boxes on 198 selected ungulate and waterfowl images (881 Canada goose, 627 milu deer, 349 Przewalski's horse, 149 Sichuan takin, 61 trumpeter swan) is released beside, not inside, the Occurrence table. Taxonomy and geometry were both reviewed; 1,552 boxes share a SAM3 proposal's geometry and 515 are human edits or additions, and the set is not filtered by the 32 px or ROI rules. The images were selected for review, so the set is not a random or exhaustive test split. Triage label accuracy against this reference set has not yet been reported.

docs.title: S9.2 Drone labels: operational table and seven-video reference set
docs.text:
Operational table. The 318,203 machine drone Occurrences remain first-generation labels: a SAM3 box on every 15th frame with a top-1 BioCLIP Tree-of-Life taxon. The only measured accuracy for that labeler comes from human-annotated camera-trap subsets:

Analysis Level n Precision Recall F1 / accuracy SAM3 animal localization, camera traps IoU ≥ 0.50 1,125 0.866 0.845 0.856 Tree-of-Life taxonomic assignment class 951 0.845 order 951 0.660 family 951 0.463 genus 951 0.322 species 951 0.271

Usable statement: class-rank labels support screening and triage; species-rank labels require curation; anything aggregating across ranks is uninterpretable. A single headline accuracy anywhere in the 0.27–0.85 range would mislead. Corroborating evidence: the taxonomy crosswalk holds 12,577 label keys, of which only 4 consist entirely of expert-verified records and 16 contain accepted names with mixed verification evidence.

Seven-video reference set. Seven drone videos were human-annotated on 1,089 sampled frames for four focal classes, with onager observations excluded: 20250703_parrotanafi_1, _2, _5 (C1), 20250811_DJI_01, 20250818_parrot_01, _02, and 20250825_parrot_01 (C2). The corrected reference holds 27,159 four-class boxes (the localization audit below was run against 27,180 before the final manual review): Père David's deer 21,177, Sichuan takin 3,293, Przewalski's horse 2,066, Canada goose 644. It is delivered as COCO JSON with provenance, a frame-to-proposal mapping, and the audit files.

SAM3 localization against the reference (35,312 proposals, one-to-one matching):

IoU Precision Recall F1 0.25 0.758 0.985 0.856 0.50 0.749 0.973 0.847 0.75 0.740 0.961 0.836

Per-class recall at IoU 0.25: Przewalski's horse 0.961, Père David's deer 0.985, Sichuan takin 0.993, Canada goose 1.000. Per-video recall at IoU 0.25 ranges from 0.958 (20250818_parrot_02) to 0.999 (20250825_parrot_01).

Resolve–Clear–Defer prototype triage was then run over the full proposal pool (seed 3, density-moderated k-center acquisition, calibrated rule k = 5, τ_fg = 4, τ_bg = 4). It spent 100 proposals on calibration and 1,610 on expert review (4.6% of the 35,212-proposal evaluation pool), handled the remaining 33,602 automatically, and got 28,040 of those right: 79.6% of the evaluation pool, or 83.5% of the automatic decisions. Zero proposals were left deferred.

Four-species classification on the 25,897 matched, unreviewed foreground instances (78.4% Père David's deer, so always-deer scores 0.784 accuracy):

Method Precision Recall F1 Accuracy Macro-F1 Prototype triage, automatic decisions only 0.913 0.850 0.880 0.850 0.789 BioCLIP 2 zero-shot, four prompts 0.167 0.167 0.167 0.167 0.230 Tree-of-Life, open-world, exact focal-taxon match 0.947 0.037 0.071 0.037 0.188

Species-wise recall for triage: Père David's deer 0.918, Przewalski's horse 0.687, Canada goose 0.590, Sichuan takin 0.551. The dominant automatic errors are wrong-species resolves into Père David's deer (takin 1,287, horse 595, goose 100) and 1,584 deer cleared as background. Read the table carefully: Tree-of-Life is evaluated open-world, so its 0.037 recall is exact top-1 recognition of a focal taxon under an unconstrained vocabulary, not animal recognition accuracy; BioCLIP 2 zero-shot always answers one of four prompts and has no background option; triage abstentions count as no prediction. All figures are proposal-level repeated observations from seven videos, not independent animals.

Manual European starling supplement. Twelve human-added Sturnus vulgaris boxes on one frame (20250703_parrotanafi_2 / VID_002, frame 1320) were appended to the drone Occurrence table on 2026-11-01 with basisOfRecord = HumanObservation, identificationVerificationStatus = human-supported; limited-resolution, and remarks stating that no SAM3 proposal, embedding, or triage decision was involved. The identification rests on limited pixels in a single frame and should be interpreted cautiously. These records are excluded from the 27,159-box reference, the localization audit, the triage calibration and evaluation, and the species-classification comparison; none of the numbers above change if they are dropped. The 12 rows were appended twice (24 rows, 12 distinct occurrenceIDs) in both the drone and merged tables (defect 21, repaired in the release build).

docs.title: S9.4 Why this must be published
docs.text:
1. A taxon string is not reproducible without the model that produced it. Two versions of the same classifier yield different taxa from the same image.
  2. Published uncertainty is what makes labels re-derivable. Machine labels are a snapshot of a model, not ground truth. A release that keeps source media, detection geometry, model identity, and per-rank accuracy can be re-labeled when better models arrive and the label sets compared meaningfully. One shipping only final taxon strings cannot.
  3. Aggregate accuracy hides the rank-dependent failure mode above.
  4. Verification status must be per record, not per dataset — a README caveat cannot be filtered on.

docs.text:
Derived from the Campaign-2 Jotform logs in thewilds_20250804_20250828/jotforms/ (two camera-trap exports, two bioacoustic exports). Every row is one sensor servicing action with a DateTime stamp, site ID, device ID, SD-card ID, team member, and free-text note.

Trip Actions Window Elapsed Median gap between actions People 2025-08-04 8 08:58–10:41 103 min 16.0 min 3 2025-08-07 6 08:59–10:05 66 min 3.0 min 1 2025-08-11 9 09:32–10:48 76 min 3.0 min 2 Total 23 245 min (4.1 h)

Breakdown of the 23 actions: 11 dropoff (deployment), 6 pickup (retrieval), 5 check-in (status only, no SD or battery swap), 1 combined. By modality: 12 acoustic, 11 camera.

Additional operational fields captured per action:

  • Access difficulty, 1–3 scale — recorded on 15 of 23 actions (rating 3: 9 actions; rating 1: 5; rating 2: 1)
  • Battery status — e.g. 98%, 95%, 60%, "Low", "100%"
  • SD-card storage — e.g. "7% full", "26% full", "5GB"
  • Camera heading — compass octant, used by the camera-trap georeferencing
  • Relocation notes — free text landmarks ("Zebra shelter", "Zip tower", "Lake trail"), which is how the TW09-CT02 mid-deployment move was recovered
  • Team member name and email

Scope boundary: this is measured elapsed field time for the three retained mid-campaign Jotform exports only. Campaign-1 field notes have no clock times, Aug. 28 retrieval submissions are absent from the retained exports, and no per-stage analyst-time log exists. The release therefore reports no total campaign field effort and no measured desk-processing hours.

Coverage limits. These exports cover the three mid-campaign trips only. Campaign-1 field notes (thewilds_20250630_20250703/field_notes/*.md) are narrative and contain no clock times, and the 2025-08-28 retrieval visits do not appear in the exported forms. So 4.1 h is logged servicing time, not total field effort.

Not recorded anywhere: analyst time per processing stage. Field visits were logged with timestamps; the timestamp-repair and taxonomy-review work was not. This asymmetry is requirement R7 in the paper.

docs.title: S14.1 Release discipline
docs.text:
Integration passes are dated and immutable. Every mutation retains a before-copy and emits a JSON audit record. Passes differ semantically, not just additively — different visual-label semantics, corrected timestamps — so comparing numbers across passes is invalid in a way that is not visible in the numbers. Any figure or table must name the release build it was computed from.

The 2026-10-22 release build supersedes the 2026-07-24 pass; each of its repairs (S10, S3, S4, S16) has its own JSON audit record, shipped under metadata/provenance/. The 2026-09-20 curated-bird update is reconstructible from:

docs.title: S16. Defect inventory, in full
docs.text:
Every defect class found while integrating the SmartWilds campaigns (release build 2026-10-22; camera tables updated 2026-11-08). docs.title: The Milu-deer activity project
docs.text: The camera-trap and acoustic analysis on the legacy branches belongs to a separate project by Bharath Pillai and Varun Viswapriyan on annotation-free verification of Milu (Père David's) deer activity, using deer calls and distance estimation. It has a workshop paper, Cross-Modal Corroboration for Annotation-Free Wildlife Monitoring, and a journal paper under review. That work uses its own labels and its own acoustic model; the holistic dataset documented here uses a substantially updated labeling protocol (see the camera-trap release note). The two are kept separate on purpose, and the numbers in this release should not be read as inputs to or outputs of that paper.

docs.title: Using agents on your own data
Using agents on your own data
docs.text: The SmartWilds documentation was produced with LLM coding agents working in the project's file system under the authors' direction (how we used them). This page is the practical version: how to set an agent up on a field archive, what to give it, and prompts that worked.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Run the agent where the data is. A coding agent (we used Claude Code) needs read access to the archive and write access to a documentation directory. On a shared cluster, start it in the project directory on a login or interactive node; it only lists directories, reads text and metadata, and runs small scripts.
  2. Give it a project file. A CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md) at the root describing the layout, the modalities, the naming conventions, and where notes go saves re-explaining every session. Ours is a page long.
  3. Put the standards in context. Download the FAIR² Drones template and quick-start checklist and the Imageomics dataset card template into a documentation/guidelines/ directory and tell the agent to follow them. See Guidelines to give the agent.
  4. Keep the archive read-only. Agents propose; people decide. Every change to a released table should leave a dated before-copy and a JSON audit record.

docs.title: Tasks and prompts
docs.text:
Inventory a campaign directorySummarize the recordsFind discrepanciesTurn checks into QA/QC scriptsDraft a dataset cardKeep documentation in sync 
Walk thewilds_20250804_20250828/ and write
thewilds_20250804_20250828_data_report.md. For each modality and
deployment: file counts and sizes by type, the metadata and log files
present, the naming convention, date range of the files, and anything
that looks wrong (clock reporting an impossible year, missing telemetry,
empty folders, duplicate files). List the people named in the logs.
Use the directory-tree style of the campaign-1 report.

From occurrences.csv and events.csv in <dir>, tabulate: Events by
eventType; Occurrences by deployment, by taxon (class and species rank),
by identificationVerificationStatus, and by campaign; date range per
table; share of records with coordinates, times, and associatedMedia.
Write the result as Markdown tables I can paste into the supplement.
Compute from the tables; do not copy numbers from existing prose.

Cross-check two things that should agree and report every mismatch:
(1) the raw WAV inventory against the AudioRecording Events;
(2) each Occurrence's eventDate against its parent Event's span;
(3) sentinel strings (nan, None, -1, 1970-01-01) in any date, time, or
coordinate column; (4) duplicate occurrenceID values; (5) associatedMedia
paths that do not resolve. For each finding: scope (how many rows, which
deployments), what detected it, and candidate repairs. Do not repair.

Turn the checks we just ran into a read-only audit script
(scripts/validation/audit_darwin_core_snapshot.py) that takes a table
directory and writes a JSON and a Markdown report. Standard library only.
Exit non-zero on any ERROR finding. Include the merged-table parity check.

Draft the dataset card for the bioacoustics tables following
documentation/guidelines/TEMPLATE.md (FAIR² Drones) and the Imageomics
card template. Fill every section from the tables, sensor_configurations.md,
and the field notes; leave a visible TODO where the information is not in
the repository rather than inventing it. Front matter: license, tags,
size_categories, Darwin Core coverage dates and representative point.

The drone Occurrence table changed (12 duplicate rows dropped). Find every
number in docs/, metadata/, and README.md that depends on it, update the
ones you can recompute from the new table, and list the ones you cannot.

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text:
Agent output is a draft until a person has checked it. What we check:

  • Numbers come from the tables. Ask the agent to show the computation (a code cell or a one-line script), and spot-check against an independent count.
  • Nothing was invented. Empty template sections should say what is missing and why (see S8 of the supplement), not be filled in plausibly.
  • Repairs are proposed, not applied. The author chooses the repair; the agent implements it with a before-copy and an audit record.
  • Grant language is verbatim. Funder acknowledgements, award numbers, and the disclaimer are copied exactly from guidelines/ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md, never paraphrased.
  • Tone and spelling. Direct statements, American English, no venue names in dataset documentation while a paper is under review.
  • Paths and identifiers. No cluster paths or internal snapshot names in anything public; scripts read locations from environment variables.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text: With the standards in context the agent produces cards and inventories in the expected structure on the first pass, and review effort goes into checking numbers and wording rather than restructuring. The agents found most of the rows in the defect inventory by cross-checking artifacts that should agree; the "Detected by" column records what made each defect visible.

docs.title: Guidelines to give the agent
docs.text:
Prompting with the documentation standards we wanted to follow, rather than describing the desired output from scratch, was the single biggest time saver. These are the documents we kept in the agent's context (or packaged as a reusable skill) for every documentation task.

Resource Use FAIR² Drones Data Standard (repository): TEMPLATE.md, QUICKSTART_GUIDE.md Dataset card structure and required metadata for drone and multi-sensor wildlife datasets: Darwin Core Event and Occurrence fields, platform and sensor metadata, annotation and quality fields Imageomics dataset card template, part of the Imageomics Guide (Campolongo et al., 2026) Base card template for biodiversity and computer-vision datasets, which the FAIR² template extends guidelines/ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md The funder acknowledgements and disclaimer, to be copied verbatim, never paraphrased Hugging Face dataset cards YAML front matter and card conventions Darwin Core terms Term definitions for Events and Occurrences, so column names, event types, and the verification-status vocabulary follow the standard KABR behavior telemetry dataset A completed FAIR² Drones card and processing scripts to imitate The project's own field notes, sensor configuration tables, and processing logs The facts

FAIR² Drones quick-start checklist

docs.title: FAIR² Drone Dataset Card: Quick-Start Guide
docs.text:
For researchers creating or documenting drone-based wildlife datasets

Below is a streamlined checklist for creating a WildFAIRx compliant drone dataset card. Review the full dataset card template for detailed guidance.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• [ ] Gather image/video files and annotation files (if applicable)
  • [ ] Collect drone/sensor specifications (model numbers)
  • [ ] Locate flight logs or mission notes
  • [ ] Find research permits and approval numbers
  • [ ] Create species list with scientific names (use GBIF)
  • [ ] Set aside 2-3 hours for completion

docs.title: Choose Your Template
docs.text:
Select the appropriate template based on your primary use case:

  • Object Detection: Detection Template (~2 hours) - Core + Darwin Core + COCO annotations
  • Multi-Object Tracking: Tracking Template (~2.5 hours) - Detection + MOT format + ID protocols
  • Behavior Recognition: Behavior Template (~3 hours) - Detection + Ethogram + temporal labels
  • Robotics Benchmarking: Platform Template (~2.5 hours) - Core + Full telemetry + Minimal annotations
  • Multiple Tasks: Comprehensive Template (~3-4 hours) - All modules

docs.title: YAML Front Matter
docs.text:
• [ ] License: Specify license type (e.g., cc-by-4.0)
  • [ ] Pretty Name: Provide descriptive dataset name
  • [ ] Task Categories: List relevant tasks (e.g., object-detection, image-classification)
  • [ ] Tags: Include relevant tags (e.g., wildlife-monitoring, species names, locations)
  • [ ] Size Categories: Specify dataset size (e.g., n<1k, 1k<n<10k)

docs.title: Dataset Overview
docs.text:
• [ ] Title: Clear, descriptive title
  • [ ] Description: 2-3 paragraph summary of dataset purpose and content
  • [ ] Authors: List curators/authors with affiliations
  • [ ] Contact Information: Provide contact details or point to discussion forum
  • [ ] Repository: Link to GitHub repository
  • [ ] Homepage: Provide link if available
  • [ ] DOI: Assign or note as pending

docs.title: Data Structure
docs.text:
• [ ] Directory Structure: Document file organization with tree diagram
  • [ ] File Formats: List formats for images (e.g., JPG, PNG) and annotations (e.g., COCO JSON, YOLO)
  • [ ] Naming Convention: Explain file naming pattern with examples
  • [ ] Data Splits: Describe train/val/test splits with counts and creation method
  • [ ] Example Files: Link to at least one representative image

Consistent Naming Conventions

Ensure file naming is consistent across videos, telemetry files, and occurrence data: - Use the same date format throughout (e.g., YYYY_MM_DD or DD_MM_YY) - Match session/flight identifiers exactly between CSV files and data folders - Document any naming changes (e.g., session_1 → flight_1) to maintain data linkages - Test that scripts can locate files using your naming pattern

docs.title: Event Records
docs.text:
For each survey location/date, document:

  • [ ] eventID: Unique identifier per mission
  • [ ] eventDate: Date in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)
  • [ ] eventTime: Time with timezone
  • [ ] decimalLatitude/Longitude: Coordinates in WGS84
  • [ ] coordinateUncertaintyInMeters: GPS accuracy (typically 5-10m)
  • [ ] locality: Study site description
  • [ ] habitat: Habitat type
  • [ ] samplingProtocol: Survey method (e.g., "UAV transect at 60m AGL")
  • [ ] sampleSizeValue/Unit: Coverage area and units
  • [ ] samplingEffort: Duration or effort metric

Extracting GPS Data from Telemetry

If your videos have embedded telemetry (SRT files, EXIF data, or flight logs), you can extract GPS coordinates programmatically: - Use exiftool for EXIF GPS data from images - Parse DJI .SRT files for frame-level GPS coordinates - Extract launch points, min/max bounds, and altitude ranges - Aggregate video-level data to session/mission-level events - See KABR scripts for Python examples

docs.title: Occurrence Records
docs.text:
• [ ] Scientific Names: Verify all species names with authority via GBIF
  • [ ] Taxonomic Hierarchy: Complete Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species for each taxon
  • [ ] Occurrence Table: Create table linking events to species observations

docs.title: Platform Specifications
docs.text:
• [ ] Platform Type: Drone type (multirotor, fixed-wing, hybrid)
  • [ ] Manufacturer and Model: Full platform identification
  • [ ] Physical Specs: Weight, dimensions, flight time, max speed, wind resistance
  • [ ] Sensor Details: Camera manufacturer, model, resolution, sensor size, focal length, field of view
  • [ ] Additional Sensors: List any thermal, LiDAR, multispectral sensors
  • [ ] Gimbal: Type and axes of stabilization
  • [ ] Autonomy Mode: Manual, waypoint, or fully autonomous
  • [ ] Flight Features Used: Grid, orbit, follow, terrain-following, etc.

docs.title: Mission Parameters
docs.text:
• [ ] Flight Altitude: Range in meters AGL
  • [ ] Flight Speed: Speed in m/s
  • [ ] Flight Pattern: Description (grid, transect, adaptive)
  • [ ] Coverage: Area covered per mission
  • [ ] Image Overlap: Forward/side overlap percentages
  • [ ] Environmental Conditions: Weather, temperature, wind, visibility
  • [ ] Telemetry Data: Available flight logs and formats (GPS, IMU, battery, etc.)
  • [ ] Permits: Research permits, IRB/IACUC approvals, aviation regulations followed
  • [ ] Animal Welfare: Minimum altitudes, disturbance protocols

docs.title: Format and Coverage
docs.text:
• [ ] Supported Tasks: Detection, tracking, segmentation, behavior, re-ID, keypoints
  • [ ] Annotation Format: Specify format for each task (COCO, MOT, etc.)
  • [ ] Label Set: List all classes/species, behaviors, attributes
  • [ ] Total Counts: Images, annotations, annotations per image (min/max/avg)
  • [ ] Per-Class Distribution: Count per class/species

docs.title: Quality Metrics
docs.text:
• [ ] Creation Method: Manual, semi-automatic, or automatic
  • [ ] Annotation Tool: Software used (CVAT, Label Studio, etc.)
  • [ ] Annotators: Who created annotations (experts, students, crowd workers)
  • [ ] Quality Assurance: Number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, review process
  • [ ] Confidence Scores: Whether included in annotation files
  • [ ] Known Issues: Annotation gaps, difficult cases, systematic biases

docs.title: Annotation Difficulty
docs.text:
• [ ] Occlusion: Percentage of instances with none/partial/heavy occlusion
  • [ ] Crowd Density: Distribution across sparse/moderate/dense scenarios
  • [ ] Scale Variation: Range of object sizes
  • [ ] Environmental Challenges: Glare, shadows, motion blur, etc.

docs.title: Dataset Statistics
docs.text:
• [ ] Temporal Coverage: Date range, seasons represented
  • [ ] Spatial Coverage: Number of locations, total area surveyed
  • [ ] Class Balance: Distribution across classes/species
  • [ ] Baseline Results: Performance metrics if available

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
• [ ] Known Biases: Geographic, temporal, species, environmental
  • [ ] Limitations: Technical constraints, coverage gaps, quality issues
  • [ ] Recommendations: Guidance for appropriate dataset use
  • [ ] Ethical Considerations: Privacy, animal welfare, cultural sensitivities
  • [ ] Reporting Issues: Link to issue tracker or community forum

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
• [ ] License Details: Confirm license choice and any special conditions
  • [ ] Component Licenses: Note if images, annotations, or code have different licenses
  • [ ] Attribution Requirements: Specify how to cite the dataset

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
• [ ] Dataset Citation: Provide BibTeX entry for the dataset
  • [ ] Associated Paper: Include citation for related publications

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text:
• [ ] Funding Sources: List grants and funding agencies
  • [ ] Contributors: Acknowledge field teams, annotators, collaborators
  • [ ] Institutional Support: Note supporting organizations

docs.title: Optional Sections
docs.text:
• [ ] Glossary: Define technical terms or specialized calculations
  • [ ] Additional Information: Any other relevant context
  • [ ] Related Datasets: Links to complementary datasets
  • [ ] Multimodal Linkages: Connections to other sensor data

docs.title: WildFAIRx Compliance
docs.text:
• [ ] DOI assigned or pending
  • [ ] License clearly stated
  • [ ] All required (*) fields completed in template
  • [ ] Machine-readable YAML front matter filled
  • [ ] Contact information provided

docs.title: Darwin Core Compliance
docs.text:
• [ ] Event records complete (dates, locations, protocol)
  • [ ] Occurrence records have scientific names with authorities
  • [ ] Taxonomic hierarchy filled (minimum to family level)
  • [ ] Sampling effort quantified
  • [ ] Coordinates in WGS84 with uncertainty

docs.title: Practical Completeness
docs.text:
• [ ] Directory structure documented
  • [ ] File naming convention explained
  • [ ] Data splits clearly defined
  • [ ] Annotation format specified
  • [ ] At least one example image linked
  • [ ] Known limitations acknowledged

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
Vague Descriptions ❌ "We used a drone to collect wildlife images" ✓ "DJI Matrice 300 RTK with Zenmuse H20T camera flew grid patterns at 60m AGL"

Missing Geographic Precision ❌ "Collected in Tanzania" ✓ "Serengeti National Park, Mara Region (-2.3456, 34.8123 ±5m)"

Unclear Sampling Effort ❌ "Multiple flights" ✓ "45 missions totaling 30 flight hours, covering 2,500 hectares"

Incomplete Species Names ❌ "elephants, zebras, giraffes" ✓ "Loxodonta africana, Equus quagga, Giraffa camelopardalis"

Undocumented Splits ❌ "Split into train/val/test" ✓ "Stratified by location and season: missions 1-300 (train), 301-350 (val), 351-400 (test)"

Hidden Biases ❌ "Representative wildlife dataset" ✓ "Dry season only; large-bodied species overrepresented; morning flights bias against nocturnal species"

docs.title: Time-Saving Tips
docs.text:
Before Starting: - Gather all information before opening the template - Copy from existing paper methods sections - Look up drone/camera specs online from manufacturer sites

While Completing: - Start with easy sections (Overview, Structure) to build momentum - Mark sections to revisit with TODO notes - Use EXIF data from images for missing camera/GPS information - Estimate reasonably if exact values unavailable (note as approximations)

Automation Opportunities: - Write scripts to extract GPS/altitude from telemetry files (SRT, EXIF, flight logs) - Generate occurrence records from detection annotations - Calculate statistics (image counts, annotation distributions) programmatically - Aggregate frame-level or video-level data to session-level events - Validate Darwin Core format compliance automatically

For Missing Information: - Document what's unavailable rather than leaving blank - Contact original research team if retrofitting dataset - Use "not available" or "not recorded" explicitly

docs.text:
Questions, Comments, or Concerns?

For assistance: - Report issues or unclear sections via GitHub Issues - Contribute example cards or improvements - Share feedback on the template

Ready to start?

  1. Download the appropriate template for your task
  2. Gather your information using the checklist above
  3. Set aside 2-3 hours to complete the card

docs.title: Packaging as a skill
docs.text:
The guidelines are small enough to include verbatim. A minimal skill directory for a coding agent:

skills/dataset-documentation/
├── SKILL.md            # when to use, the steps, the review checklist
├── TEMPLATE.md         # FAIR² Drones dataset card template
├── QUICKSTART_GUIDE.md # FAIR² Drones checklist

docs.title: Cross-modal coordination: planning a sensing system from its metadata
docs.text:
Distributed sensing systems are expensive to deploy. A camera-trap network, a set of acoustic recorders, drone flights, and visitor photographs each cost field time, hardware, and compute, and once deployed they are hard to change. Yet the planning tools that other infrastructure takes for granted, the ones that tell you which hardware tier, which sensor configuration, which model, and which filtering threshold a deployment needs before you build it, do not exist for ecological sensing. Systems get sized by rule of thumb and corrected in the field.

The metadata in this release is what makes such tools possible. Fine-grained timestamps, sensor configurations, and confidence-scored detections, aligned across modalities, are enough to characterize each modality's workload, to synthesize the workload a coordinated multi-modal system would produce, and to predict whether a given hardware tier can keep up. The paper A Blueprint for Cross-Modal Coordination at the Far Edge (Kline, Potlapally, Cheng, Berger-Wolf, Subramoni, Stewart; to appear) develops that method on the SmartWilds metadata, and analysis/cross_modal_coordination/ is its code and derived data, included here as a worked example of what the metadata enables.

Paper abstract

Multimodal autonomous systems deployed in challenging far-edge settings, such as precision agriculture, search-and-rescue, wildfire and disaster response, and ecological monitoring, collect heterogeneous data streams whose combined signal exceeds the sum of their parts. This opens an action space in which one modality's inference can direct another's sampling to concentrate scarce compute, bandwidth, and energy where the signal is richest. Realizing this cross-modal coordination at the edge, however, is a challenging coupled-provisioning problem: hardware, sensor configuration, model choice, and data-filtering thresholds each shape the joint workload and depend on it in turn, and the workload cannot be measured until a coordinated deployment exists, which is prohibitively costly to iterate in remote field settings. We propose a record-characterize-synthesize approach that probes such future systems by leveraging co-located, temporally aligned single-modality deployments as a proxy for the spatiotemporal conditions of a cross-modal deployment. We apply our approach to a 24-day multimodal field deployment whose preserved metadata schema (temporal alignment, spatial registration, and inferential confidence across all streams) supports cross-modal workload reasoning that existing multimodal benchmark datasets cannot. We report the findings from the workload characterization and synthesis, providing a blueprint for feasible cross-modal field deployments. This work scopes cross-modal coordination at the edge as a distinct systems domain and lays empirical groundwork for the next generation of mission-driven multi-modal autonomous system deployments.

docs.title: The method: record, characterize, synthesize
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  R[Record<br/>co-located single-modality<br/>deployments] --> C[Characterize<br/>per-modality workload model<br/>rate, burstiness, co-occurrence, throughput]
  C --> S[Synthesize<br/>a coordinated multi-modal trace<br/>from a recipe and a seed]
  S --> P[Predict<br/>hardware tier x policy<br/>feasibility grid]
Phase What it produces Where Characterize Workload model per modality: change-point arrival rates, burstiness, diurnal profile, cross-modal co-occurrence scripts/01_characterize/, shipped as data/primitives/ Synthesize A synthetic multi-modal trace from a recipe: which modalities, how one modality's detections re-shape another's sampling (interleave, conditional scaling, prior injection), at what intensity scripts/02_synthesize/ Case studies Four coordination scenarios: acoustic detection triggers cameras; a camera triggers a drone; a focal camera re-tunes its neighbors; citizen-science reports act as priors for everything scripts/03_case_studies/ Fidelity Does synthesis stay within the natural variation of the recorded sites? Identity test, variance envelope, topology scaling, intensity sweep scripts/04_fidelity/ Feasibility Predicted hardware tier × inference policy grid for each case study, calibrated against one measured cell scripts/05_feasibility/ Figures and supplement The paper's figures and the tables cut from it scripts/figures/, supplement/

Synthesis is deterministic: the same recipe and seed always produce the same trace. The identity recipe re-emits the recorded event counts within 0.1 to 4.3 percent for every modality.

docs.title: What it says about the metadata
docs.text:
• Burstiness is a joint property of modality and deployment topology. Camera-trap and drone arrivals have burstiness above 0.5, so provisioning must be for peak rate, not mean rate, and adding sites changes burstiness in a modality-specific way. None of this is visible without second-level, corrected timestamps.
  • Cross-modal co-occurrence is low at the hour scale (all pairwise Jaccard below 0.05), which licenses treating modalities as independent in synthesis and is itself a finding about how these sensors sample the landscape.
  • Feasibility verdicts depend on sensor configuration. The acoustic recorder's schedule (hourly versus dawn-and-dusk chorus) changes the response tier a camera network needs; the camera's photo-versus-video mode changes the detection pipeline's load. The sensor configurations in metadata/sensor_configurations.md are inputs to the model, not footnotes.
  • A field laptop is the limiting tier under tight latency targets, and the one measured cell confirmed the prediction within 23 percent.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
cd analysis/cross_modal_coordination
pip install -r requirements.txt
./run_all.sh                          # identity synthesis, four case studies, fidelity checks
for f in scripts/figures/fig_*.py; do python3 "$f"; done   # the paper's figures

No archive access is needed: the shipped workload primitives are enough to synthesize all four modalities. Read REPRODUCIBILITY.md first; it lists what reproduces exactly, what needs the field archive, and which published numbers carry caveats. supplement/README.md holds the tables and figures cut from the camera-ready.

docs.title: Joining the modalities in space and time
docs.text: The point of the release is that four independently collected modalities can be put on the same spatial and temporal footing. This page says which columns do that, what their precision is, and where the traps are. A runnable example is at examples/join_camera_acoustic_by_site_hour.py.

docs.title: Temporal keys
docs.text:
Column Tables Meaning eventDate, eventTime all Occurrence tables Local date and time of the record. Camera-trap values are the corrected timestamps, not the camera clock. An eventDate interval (start/end) means the record is only known to lie in that span corrected_timestamp, correction_method, correction_confidence images.csv (camera traps) Per-image corrected capture time, the method that produced it (18 methods, supplement S5), and its confidence timestampPrecision, timeEligible arrival traces second or day; whether the record can enter inter-arrival statistics

Three temporal traps

  • Camera clocks were wrong on 93.9% of images (defect 1). Use the corrected values; the burned-in overlay in the image shows the raw clock.
  • The 2025-08-11 drone flights have a date but no time (defect 15): their eventTime is blank and they cannot be placed within the day.
  • Acoustic Events are recording windows, not instants: a 5- or 15-minute WAV. An acoustic Occurrence's time is the recording start.

Campaign windows: June 30 – July 3 (campaign 1), August 4 – 28 (campaign 2), September 8 (campaign 3). The deployment Events carry each sensor's actual eventDate interval, which is the right denominator for effort.

docs.title: Spatial keys
docs.text:
Modality locationID Coordinates Uncertainty Camera traps Site code TW01 … TW11 Deployment Event: camera position. Occurrences inherit the site; animal positions are not inferred in the released table 5 m Bioacoustics Site code Deployment Event: recorder position 50 m Drones Flight identifier (20250818_parrot_01) Deployment Event: flight centroid; MediaEvent: video position; Occurrences: ground-projected box position where georef_status = ok 100 m (flight), per-row for projections Citizen science none Park-level point on the observation session 5,000 m

Fixed sensors are joined by site code and campaign, because several sensors moved between campaigns (the TW07 recorder, the TW09 camera after August 18; defect 6). Drones and citizen science have no site code and are joined by coordinates or by date.

Site codes are shared across modalities. In campaign 2, camera traps and recorders were co-located at TW02, TW06, and TW09; the supplemental material (S2, S3) lists every deployment with its coordinates and dates.

docs.title: The Event hierarchy
docs.text: All tables share one hierarchy rooted at TheWilds_2025. Walking parentEventID from an Occurrence's eventID reaches the deployment (or flight, or session), then the modality's Project, then the study root. That is how an Occurrence finds its campaign, its sensor configuration, and its deployment coordinates.

docs.title: Example: camera and acoustic co-occurrence by site-hour
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

def load(root):
    ev = pd.read_csv(f"{root}/events.csv", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)
    oc = pd.read_csv(f"{root}/occurrences.csv", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)
    return ev, oc

cam_ev, cam = load("darwin_core/smartwilds-camera-traps")
aru_ev, aru = load("darwin_core/smartwilds-bioacoustics")

# 1. Temporal key: corrected local timestamp, truncated to the hour.
for df in (cam, aru):
    df["t"] = pd.to_datetime(df.eventDate + " " + df.eventTime, errors="coerce")
    df["hour"] = df.t.dt.floor("h")

# 2. Spatial key: the site code on fixed sensors (TW01 ... TW11), plus the
#    campaign window from the deployment Event, because a few sensors moved
#    between campaigns.
def campaign(ev):
    dep = ev[ev.eventType == "SensorDeployment"].set_index("eventID")
    return dep.eventDate.str.slice(0, 7)          # "2025-06" or "2025-08"
cam["campaign"] = cam.eventID.map(cam_ev.set_index("eventID").parentEventID).map(campaign(cam_ev))
aru["campaign"] = aru.eventID.map(aru_ev.set_index("eventID").parentEventID).map(campaign(aru_ev))

# 3. Co-occurrence per site-hour: camera detections next to acoustic detections.
cam_h = cam.dropna(subset=["hour"]).groupby(["campaign", "locationID", "hour"]).size().rename("camera_occurrences")
aru_h = aru.dropna(subset=["hour"]).groupby(["campaign", "locationID", "hour"]).size().rename("acoustic_occurrences")
joined = pd.concat([cam_h, aru_h], axis=1).fillna(0).astype(int)
both = joined[(joined.camera_occurrences > 0) & (joined.acoustic_occurrences > 0)]
print(f"site-hours with both modalities: {len(both):,} of {len(joined):,}")
print(both.reset_index().groupby("locationID").size().rename("site_hours_with_both").to_string())

On the current tables this reports 403 site-hours (of 2,299 with any detection) in which both a camera and a recorder at the same site produced Occurrences, at TW02, TW06, and TW09.

docs.title: Using the data correctly
docs.text:
Pick a verification floor before analysis

Almost every Occurrence is a machine label, and the status vocabulary differs by table. Camera-trap labels carry a labelProvenance (triage_resolved, triage_reviewed, triage_forced_1nn, human-edit, human-reviewed); drone and acoustic labels are unverified or validated; the 12 human-added drone starling boxes are human-supported; limited-resolution. The drone labels come from BioCLIP 2 (the TreeOfLife-200M model, imageomics/bioclip-2) run in its open-world Tree of Life mode, which predicts a taxon with its full rank hierarchy rather than choosing among a fixed label list; species-rank accuracy on human-annotated subsets is 0.271 and class-rank accuracy is 0.845 (supplement, S9).

  • Occurrences are detection crops, not individuals. Bursts and adjacent drone frames repeat the same animal.
  • Use the corrected timestamps. Camera clocks were wrong on most deployments, and burned-in overlays show the raw clock. Every image carries its correction method and confidence (images.csv).
  • A zero occurrence_count is not evidence of absence.
  • Report your choices. State the unit of observation, the verification floor, and the timestamp policy alongside any derived metric.

docs.title: Arrival traces
docs.text:
scripts/arrival_traces/generate_arrival_traces_v2.py derives the Campaign-2 (August 4–28, 2025) arrival streams used in the systems analysis from the Darwin Core tables. It has no arguments: run it from the scripts/ directory of a table set, and it reads ../events_all_modalities.csv, ../occurrences_all_modalities.csv, and the drone Occurrence table, and writes ../analysis/arrival_traces_v2/.

cd "$SMARTWILDS_DWC_OUT"/scripts
python generate_arrival_traces_v2.py

Two layers, one stream per modality:

Layer Unit of arrival Streams Acquisition One recording or image capture acoustic_wav_recording, camera_image_capture Inference One retained Occurrence camera_operational_occurrence, bioacoustic_machine_occurrence, drone_machine_detection_crop, citizen_science_curated_occurrence

Every output row links back to its source Event or Occurrence (sourceID), carries a second-level timestamp and a timeEligible flag (date-only records are kept but excluded from inter-arrival statistics), and names the release it came from. arrival_trace_contract_v2.json records, per stream, the unit, inclusion rule, date window, counts, rate, coefficient of variation, and burstiness; input_manifest_v2.json carries SHA-256 checksums of inputs and outputs.

Rates are time-eligible arrivals divided by the fixed 600-hour window; CV is the population standard deviation over the mean of successive inter-arrival intervals; burstiness is B = (CV - 1) / (CV + 1). The arrival statistics are in the supplemental material.

docs.title: Darwin Core generation
docs.text: scripts/darwin_core/ builds the Event and Occurrence tables that the whole release rests on.

docs.title: generate_darwin_core.py
docs.text:
Builds the Darwin Core tables for every modality and merges them into events_all_modalities.csv and occurrences_all_modalities.csv.

Modality Inputs What the script does Camera traps SAM3 + BioCLIP Tree-of-Life prediction CSVs, geolocated animal positions, the corrected camera timestamp map One SensorDeployment Event per camera deployment, one Occurrence per retained detection box; dates and times from the corrected timestamps Bioacoustics BirdNET result files (hourly and sunrise/sunset schedules) One AudioRecording Event per WAV, one Occurrence per recording × species with individualCount = detections; taxonomy filled from the raw results Drones Labelled detection CSVs with telemetry One SensorDeployment per flight, one MediaEvent per video, one Occurrence per detection crop Citizen science, text Their Darwin Core exports Copied into the table set

The "Tree-of-Life prediction CSVs" are the per-box outputs of BioCLIP 2 (imageomics/bioclip-2, trained on TreeOfLife-200M) in open-world Tree of Life mode: for each SAM3 box, the top-1 taxon with its rank hierarchy (kingdom to species) and the top-5 candidates, as recorded in identificationRemarks (Tree-of-Life rank, top1 score). They were produced in the external detection workspace; the code that wrote them is not in this repository.

export SMARTWILDS_ARCHIVE=/path/to/TheWilds2025
export SMARTWILDS_DWC_OUT=$SMARTWILDS_ARCHIVE/processing_output/darwin_core_release
python scripts/darwin_core/generate_darwin_core.py --force

--force overwrites an existing output directory. The script also writes QC_SUMMARY.md (row counts, distinct values, date ranges per table) and a citizen_science_media_reconciliation_*.json audit of which visitor files are referenced by Occurrences.

Hardened generation

The generator writes a fresh, non-destructive table set and never edits an existing one. Repairs to released tables (the drone nan dates, the study root Event, the WAV reconciliation) each left a *.before_* copy and a JSON audit record; the supplemental material (S10, S14) describes each.

docs.title: reconcile_bioacoustic_raw_wavs.py
docs.text:
Walks the raw WAV directories of both campaigns, matches every file to its BirdNET result and to its AudioRecording Event, and classifies each path:

  • released, with a non-empty BirdNET result;
  • processed but zero detections (header-only result): added as an Event with no Occurrences;
  • transfer duplicate (a campaign-1 file copied under a campaign-2 directory);
  • truncated or unreadable.
python scripts/darwin_core/reconcile_bioacoustic_raw_wavs.py

Writes RAW_WAV_RECONCILIATION_*.csv (one row per raw path) and .md next to the bioacoustic tables, plus the Event-repair audit JSON. This is how defect 10 in the defect inventory was found and repaired.

docs.title: Example: quickstart
docs.text:
examples/quickstart.py shows the minimum a user should do before computing anything from the tables.

pip install -r requirements.txt
python examples/quickstart.py darwin_core/smartwilds-camera-traps darwin_core/smartwilds-bioacoustics

Pass one or more dataset folders (each with data/events.csv and data/occurrences.csv, or a downloaded Hugging Face dataset). They share one Event hierarchy, so modalities can be combined. The script:

  1. Applies a verification floor. Prints the identificationVerificationStatus distribution and separates machine labels (unverified, machine-resolved) from human-reviewed ones.
  2. Joins Occurrences to Events and walks up to the deployment, then counts Occurrences per deployment.
  3. Summarizes by class rank, which is far more reliable than species rank.
  4. Extracts a drone frame if a drone dataset with data/detections.csv and its video is present: frame_index is the native frame index, so any detection can be rendered from the raw video with OpenCV.

Tip

The folders in darwin_core/ use events.csv / occurrences.csv directly (no data/ level). Either pass a downloaded dataset folder, or point the script at a folder laid out as data/events.csv.

docs.title: Georeferencing
docs.text: scripts/georeferencing/ estimates animal ground positions from detection boxes. Both scripts are provenance-heavy on purpose: every output row carries a status, so unreliable projections are flagged rather than silently mixed in.

docs.title: Camera traps: geolocate_camera_trap_treeoflife_predictions.py
docs.text:
A pinhole-model projection of the bottom-center of each box, using the camera's GPS position, bearing, horizontal field of view, and an assumed target height from camera_geolocation_config.csv. It wraps the geometry of Imageomics/camera-trap-geolocation; point CAMERA_TRAP_GEOLOCATION_SRC at its src/ directory.

export CAMERA_TRAP_GEOLOCATION_SRC=/path/to/camera-trap-geolocation/src
python scripts/georeferencing/geolocate_camera_trap_treeoflife_predictions.py \
  --input-dir  <per-camera Tree-of-Life prediction CSVs> \
  --config-csv scripts/georeferencing/camera_geolocation_config.csv \
  --output-dir <output directory> \
  [--top1-score-min 0.3] [--rank species] [--max-distance-m 500] [--overwrite]

Estimates beyond --max-distance-m are kept but flagged out_of_range.

docs.title: Drones: geolocate_drone_treeoflife_predictions.py
docs.text:
A ground-ray projection using the aircraft's telemetry (position, altitude, gimbal pitch) and per-platform field of view from drone_projection_config.csv. Each prediction row is joined back to the processed detection CSV to recover pose fields, then the box's bottom-center ray is intersected with a flat ground plane.

python scripts/georeferencing/geolocate_drone_treeoflife_predictions.py \
  --prediction-dir <per-video *.treeoflife_predictions.csv> \
  --detection-dir  <processed *_detections.csv with pose metadata> \
  --config-csv     scripts/georeferencing/drone_projection_config.csv \
  --output-dir     <output directory> \
  [--min-altitude-m 1.0] [--max-ground-range-m 300] [--min-depression-deg 2.0] [--overwrite]
georef_status Meaning ok Projected invalid_altitude Altitude below --min-altitude-m missing_drone_gps No aircraft position for the frame horizon_ray Ray too shallow (depression below --min-depression-deg) out_of_range Projected range beyond --max-ground-range-m

The method, its assumptions, and the per-platform parameters are in the supplemental material. The two configuration CSVs used for the release are shipped in this directory.

docs.title: Privacy screening
docs.text:
People appear in camera-trap images (visitors and staff), in visitor photographs, and near drone launch and landing sites. scripts/privacy_screening/ finds them with MegaDetector v5a and triages them by identifiability before release.

The rule

A person whose box is shorter than 80 px in the native image cannot be identified (the face is then under about 10 px), so the file is released as is. Any person box at or above 80 px, at confidence ≥ 0.2, sends the file to human review. Review decides: release (false positive or not identifiable) or remove. Media in which a person can be individually identified are removed from the release; drone videos are trimmed losslessly at launch and landing instead of being dropped whole.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. make_lists.py lists every camera-trap and citizen-science still (in four shards) and every video under the campaign directories, skipping the withdrawn TW07-CT05 deployment.
  2. run_screening.sh is the SLURM array job that was used: MegaDetector batch runs on the image shards and screen_videos.py on the video halves. It needs a GPU and a virtual environment with megadetector, av, and imageio-ffmpeg.
  3. screen_videos.py samples frames (every second for camera and visitor clips, every two seconds for drone videos) and writes one JSON line per frame with a person detection.
  4. triage.py turns the detector output into person_screening_images.csv and person_screening_videos.csv with a release / review decision per file, and renders crop sheets for the review queue.
  5. trim_drones.py plan proposes lossless start and end trims for drone videos whose people are within two minutes of launch or landing, and lists mid-flight people for review. trim_drones.py apply trims only the rows a reviewer has marked approved=yes, verifying each output's first frame against the source.
export SMARTWILDS_ARCHIVE=/path/to/TheWilds2025
export MEGADETECTOR_WEIGHTS=/path/to/md_v5a.0.0.pt
python scripts/privacy_screening/make_lists.py
sbatch --account=<account> scripts/privacy_screening/run_screening.sh
python scripts/privacy_screening/triage.py
python scripts/privacy_screening/trim_drones.py plan     # then review results/drone_trim_plan.csv
python scripts/privacy_screening/trim_drones.py apply

Screening evidence is carried into the release: the camera image inventory and media manifests have privacyScreeningStatus, privacyScreeningMethod, privacyHumanReviewStatus, and privacyEvidencePath columns.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
scripts/validation/audit_darwin_core_snapshot.py is a read-only integrity audit of a generated table set. Run it after generation and before release.

python scripts/validation/audit_darwin_core_snapshot.py \
  --snapshot-dir "$SMARTWILDS_DWC_OUT" \
  --stem DARWIN_CORE_AUDIT_$(date +%Y%m%d)
Check What fails it Source-to-merged parity A modality row missing from the merged tables, an extra merged row, or a value that differs between the two Event hierarchy More than one root, an orphaned parentEventID, or a cycle Occurrence links and ancestry An Occurrence whose eventID is missing, or whose Event belongs to another modality Scalars Dates, times, and coordinates that do not parse; sentinel strings such as nan, None, -1, or epoch dates Media Local associatedMedia paths that do not exist (warning) Generator drift The study root date in the generator differs from the released root Event

The audit writes <stem>.json (machine-readable findings) and <stem>.md (summary) into the table directory. It never modifies the tables.

The release build adds checks the audit does not cover, because they need the release layout: every Occurrence date inside its parent Event's span and the study window, no archive paths in any cell, and every associatedMedia value resolving to an included file in the media manifest. Those results are in each dataset's RELEASE_BUILD_AUDIT.json and summarized in the supplemental material.
